topics.title: EDLC – Embedded Product Development Life Cycle

questions.question: Explain the Embedded Product Design Life Cycle (EDLC) with diagram.
questions.answer_html:
Embedded Product Development Life Cycle (EDLC) is a structured, Analysis–Design–Implementation based problem-solving methodology for developing embedded products. It is based on the Waterfall (Linear) Model approach. It defines the interactions and activities among various groups involved in product development.

Need for EDLC

  • Understand the scope and complexity of embedded systems development.
  • Can be applied to any embedded product development.
  • Defines interaction and activities among development groups.

Three Primary Objectives of EDLC:

  1. Ensure high-quality products are delivered to the user.
  2. Risk minimization and defect prevention through project management.
  3. Maximize productivity.

Phases of EDLC

1. Need

The trigger for a new product development. Can be:

  • New or Custom Product Development
  • Product Re-engineering
  • Product Maintenance

2. Conceptualization

Defines the scope, performs cost-benefit analysis and feasibility study, and prepares project/risk management plans.

  • Feasibility Study: Examines the need and suggests possible solutions.
  • Cost Benefit Analysis (CBA): Reveals total development cost vs profit.
  • Product Scope: Defines activities involved in the product.
  • Planning Activities: Resource planning & risk management.

3. Analysis

Captures all requirements including: Functional capabilities, Performance, Operational & non-operational quality attributes, External interface requirements, Data requirements, User manuals, Maintenance requirements, General assumptions.

4. Design

Identifies application environment and creates overall architecture:

  • Preliminary Design: Top-level architecture (like a black box — inputs/outputs only). Output → Preliminary Design Document (PDD).
  • Detailed Design: Operations manual, Maintenance Manual, Training material → Detailed Design Document (DDD).

5. Development and Testing

Transforms design into a realizable product by translating detailed specifications into hardware and firmware.

  • Unit Testing – Individual modules/components tested.
  • Integration Testing – Combined modules tested together.
  • System Testing – Full system tested against requirements.
  • User Acceptance Testing (UAT) – End-user validates the product.

6. Deployment

Launching the first fully functional model — also called First Customer Shipping (FCS).

  • Notification of product deployment, training end users, product installation, post-implementation review.

7. Support

Deals with operational and maintenance of product in production environment. Includes 24×7 support, bug identification, and improvement plans.

8. Upgrades

Development of new versions (upgrades) with design modifications to fix major bugs.

9. Retirement / Disposal

Final phase — product is discontinued due to rapid technology advancement and increased user needs.

Waterfall (Linear) Model Characteristics

  • Each EDLC phase is executed in strict sequence.
  • Output of one phase → input of next phase.
  • Execution flow is unidirectional.
  • Implements extensive review systems to ensure correct process flow.
  • Bug fixes are postponed to the support phase.

Advantages:

  • Rich documentation
  • Easy project management
  • Good cost and schedule control

Drawbacks:

  • Assumes all analysis can be done without design or implementation.
  • Risk analysis is performed only once.
  • Working product available only at the end of development phase.
  • Bug fixes and corrections performed only at maintenance/support phase.

questions.question: Major steps in embedded system design (requirements, component selection, hardware and software architecture).
questions.answer_html:
Major Steps in Embedded System Design

Embedded system design follows a systematic process from requirements to deployment. The major steps are:

Step 1: Requirements Specification

Requirements specify what the system should do (functional) and how well it should do it (non-functional).
Types of Requirements:
  • Functional Requirements: What the system must do (e.g., accept payment, dispense product, calculate fare).
  • Non-Functional Requirements:
    • Input Requirements: Data from users, sensors, or other electronic systems.
    • Output Requirements: Display info, LED, sound, motor movement, printed info.
    • Performance Requirements: Response time, speed, accuracy, throughput, real-time response, reliability.
    • Power Requirements: Supply voltage, current, battery, low-power operation.
    • Memory Requirements: Flash/ROM (program), RAM (runtime data), EEPROM (persistent data).
    • Environmental Requirements: Temperature range, humidity, vibration, shock, waterproofing.
    • Size & Weight Requirements: PCB size, dimensions, enclosure.
    • Cost Requirements: Total BOM (Bill of Materials) within budget.
    • Reliability & Safety Requirements: MTBF, fail-safe mechanisms.
    • Communication Requirements: UART, I²C, SPI, CAN, USB, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, Ethernet.

Step 2: Component / Hardware Selection

Choosing the right components that satisfy specification requirements:

  • Processor/Microcontroller: Selected on processing speed, word length, RAM/Flash, I/O pins, power, peripherals, cost.
  • Sensors: Based on what physical quantity to measure (DHT11, HC-SR04, LDR, PIR, pressure). Selection: range, accuracy, resolution, response time, cost.
  • Actuators: Motors, servo motors, relays, solenoids, buzzers, LEDs.
  • Memory: Flash size, RAM, EEPROM size, speed, data retention.
  • Display & User Interface: 16×2 LCD, OLED, Touchscreen, Keypad, Push buttons.
  • Communication Interface: UART, SPI, I²C, CAN, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, Ethernet.
  • Power Supply: Input source, voltage, current rating, efficiency, battery backup.

Step 3: Hardware Architecture Design

Creating a hardware block diagram showing all components and their interconnections:

  • Identifies all hardware modules: processor, memory, sensors, actuators, communication.
  • Defines buses, interfaces and signal flows.
  • Preliminary Design → black-box (inputs/outputs defined).
  • Detailed Design → full schematic with component values.

Step 4: Software Architecture Design

Defines how the firmware/software is structured:

  • Identification of software modules and their responsibilities.
  • Use of FSM (Finite State Machine) or flowcharts to model program flow.
  • Device drivers for each hardware component (LCD driver, sensor driver, motor driver).
  • RTOS task partitioning if real-time is needed.
  • IPC mechanisms: semaphores, queues, shared memory.

Step 5: Implementation (Hardware + Firmware Development)

  • PCB design and fabrication.
  • Firmware coding in Embedded C / Assembly.
  • Integration of hardware and software.

Step 6: Testing and Debugging

  • Unit testing, integration testing, system testing, UAT.
  • Use of debuggers, emulators, simulators, logic analysers, oscilloscopes.

Step 7: Deployment and Maintenance

  • Launch (FCS — First Customer Shipping).
  • Field support, bug fixes, upgrades.

questions.question: Role of FSM and flowcharts in embedded software design, with example.
questions.answer_html:
Role of FSM and Flowcharts in Embedded Software Design

Flowcharts

A flowchart is a graphical representation of the sequential steps (algorithm) of a program using standard symbols: oval (start/end), rectangle (process), diamond (decision), parallelogram (I/O), and arrows (flow).
  • Used to plan the overall algorithm before coding.
  • Visualizes sequential, conditional, and iterative logic.
  • Helps identify missing cases or incorrect logic before implementation.

Flowchart Symbols: Oval = Start/End, Rectangle = Process, Diamond = Decision, Arrow = Flow direction.

Finite State Machine (FSM)

An FSM is a mathematical model of computation that describes the behavior of a system using a finite number of states, transitions (triggered by events/inputs), and actions (outputs). It is ideal for reactive and event-driven embedded systems.
  • FSM consists of: States, Events/Inputs, Transitions, Actions/Outputs.
  • At any time, the system is in exactly one state.
  • An event causes a transition from one state to another.
  • FSMs are used to model: vending machines, traffic lights, washing machines, protocol handlers.

FSM Example: Automatic Vending Machine

The vending machine FSM for a newspaper/chocolate vending machine (from PDF):

FSM Pseudocode (Vending Machine)

enum State { IDLE, COIN_INSERTED, SUM_COMPARE, DISPENSE, REFUND };
int sum = 0;
int cost = 5; // cost of item

State current = IDLE;

while(1) {
    switch(current) {
        case IDLE:
            if(coin_detected()) {
                sort_coin();
                current = COIN_INSERTED;
            }
            break;

        case COIN_INSERTED:
            sum += get_coin_value();
            current = SUM_COMPARE;
            break;

        case SUM_COMPARE:
            if(sum == cost)       current = DISPENSE;
            else if(sum > cost)   current = REFUND;
            else                  current = IDLE;    // need more coins
            break;

        case DISPENSE:
            dispense_item();
            sum = 0;
            current = IDLE;
            break;

        case REFUND:
            refund(sum - cost);
            dispense_item();
            sum = 0;
            current = IDLE;
            break;
    }
}

Role of FSM in Embedded Design

  • Models complex, event-driven behavior clearly and systematically.
  • Directly translatable to switch-case code in Embedded C.
  • Avoids spaghetti code — each state has clear entry/exit conditions.
  • Useful in: Protocol design, UI state management, appliance control.

questions.question: Testing and debugging methodologies; hardware testing tools, emulator, simulator, debugger; hardware and software design issues.
questions.answer_html:
Testing and Debugging Methodologies in Embedded Systems

Testing Levels

  1. Unit Testing: Individual software modules or hardware components tested in isolation.
  2. Integration Testing: Combined modules tested together to verify interfaces.
  3. System Testing: Complete assembled system tested against specified requirements.
  4. User Acceptance Testing (UAT): End-user validates the product in real-world conditions.

Hardware Testing Tools

  • Oscilloscope: Displays electrical signals vs. time. Used to check signal timing, voltage levels, waveforms.
  • Logic Analyzer: Captures and displays multiple digital signals simultaneously. Useful for protocol debugging (SPI, I²C, UART).
  • Multimeter: Measures voltage, current, resistance. Basic continuity and power checks.
  • Signal Generator: Generates test signals (sine, square, PWM) to stimulate circuits.
  • Boundary Scan / JTAG Tester: Tests PCB board connections without physical probes.
  • In-Circuit Tester (ICT): Tests individual components on a PCB while in circuit.

Emulator

An emulator is a hardware/software tool that completely replaces the target processor. It allows a developer to run, halt, single-step, and inspect the program as if on the real hardware, while providing full visibility into internal registers and memory.
  • Provides real-time control over program execution.
  • Can set hardware breakpoints and watchpoints.
  • More accurate than a simulator as it mimics real hardware timing.
  • Example: ICE (In-Circuit Emulator).

Simulator

A simulator is a software tool that models the behavior of the target hardware on a host PC. It does not require physical hardware.
  • Useful for early-stage software development before hardware is ready.
  • Can simulate peripherals, interrupts, timers.
  • Not as accurate as emulator for real-time timing.
  • Example: Proteus, QEMU, AVR Studio Simulator.

Debugger

A debugger is a tool that allows a developer to control program execution (run, pause, step), inspect variables, registers, memory, and set breakpoints.
  • Source-level debugging maps binary code back to C source.
  • JTAG-based debuggers connect directly to the target hardware.
  • Examples: GDB, OpenOCD, IAR C-SPY, Keil µVision Debugger.

Hardware Design Issues

  • Signal integrity: noise, crosstalk, ground bounce.
  • Power supply noise affecting ADC accuracy.
  • PCB layout issues: improper grounding, decoupling.
  • Timing violations: setup/hold time violations in digital circuits.
  • EMI/EMC compliance failure.
  • Wrong component rating (voltage/current).

Software Design Issues

  • Stack overflow due to insufficient stack allocation.
  • Interrupt latency problems (ISR too long).
  • Race conditions on shared variables accessed from ISR and main code.
  • Memory leaks in dynamic allocation (rarely used in embedded but risky).
  • Incorrect pointer arithmetic or buffer overflow.
  • Priority inversion in RTOS-based designs.
  • Missed real-time deadlines.
  • Uninitialized variables or watchdog timer not refreshed.

Debugging Techniques

  • printf / UART debugging: Send debug messages to serial terminal.
  • LED debugging: Toggle LEDs to indicate code execution paths.
  • Breakpoints: Halt CPU at specific instruction using JTAG/debugger.
  • Watchdog timer: Detects if system hangs and resets it.
  • Memory dump: Inspect RAM contents after a fault.
  • Code review & static analysis: MISRA-C checks, lint tools.

questions.question: Differentiate between white box and black box testing.
questions.answer_html:
Black Box vs White Box Testing

About Black Box Testing

In Black Box Testing, the functionalities of software applications are tested without having knowledge of internal code structure, implementation details, or internal paths. The tester gives input values to examine functionality and checks whether the expected output is produced.
  • Also known as: Behavioral Testing, Functional Testing, Closed-box Testing.
  • Performed by: Software Testers.
  • Tools: QTP, Selenium, LoadRunner, JMeter.

Black Box Testing Techniques

  1. Equivalence Partitioning: Divide input values into groups (classes) with the same expected outcome. Test one value from each group instead of all values.
  2. Boundary Value Analysis: Test at the edges (boundaries) of valid/invalid ranges (min, min+1, max-1, max, min-1, max+1).
  3. Decision Table Testing: Capture combinations of inputs and their system behaviors in tabular form.
  4. Error Guessing: Based on tester's experience — guess problematic areas (divide by zero, null inputs, empty submissions).
  5. State Transition Testing: Test software that changes behavior based on state when different inputs are given.
  6. All-Pairs Testing: Tests all possible discrete combinations of values (useful for checkboxes, radio buttons, list boxes).

White Box Testing

White Box Testing analyzes the internal design, code structure, and working of the software. The tester has full knowledge of the internal code/logic.
  • Also known as: Clear box testing, Open box testing, Transparent box testing, Code-based testing, Glass box testing.
  • Performed by: Software Developers.
  • Used in: Unit Testing and Integration Testing.
  • Tools: EclEmma, NUnit, PyUnit, HTMLUnit, CppUnit.
What is Verified in White Box Testing?
  • Internal security of code.
  • Poorly structured paths in coding processes.
  • Flow of specific inputs through the code.
  • Loops and decision conditions.
  • Each statement of the program.
  • Functions and modules individually.

White Box Testing Techniques

  1. Path Coverage / Testing: All possible paths from entry to exit point are defined and tested.
  2. Loop Testing: Tests all loops (while, for, do-while) — checks simple, nested, and concatenated loops; verifies loop termination condition.
  3. Branch Coverage / Condition Testing: Every logical condition (if/else) is tested for both true and false branches.
  4. Statement Coverage: Every statement in the code is executed at least once.
No. Black Box Testing White Box Testing
1Internal structure NOT known to tester. Focus on input/output.Internal structure IS known to tester.
2Functional Testing, Data-driven, Closed-box, Behavioral Testing.Structural, Glass box, Code-based, Transparent testing.
3Less programming knowledge required.Complete programming knowledge required.
4Done at higher levels: System and Acceptance testing.Done at lower levels: Unit testing and Integration testing.
5Performed by Software Testers.Performed by Developers.
6Less time-consuming.More time-consuming.
7Based on external expectations (user perspective).Based on internal coding and logic.
8Objective: Fulfill customer need.Objective: Check code quality.
9Defects identified once code is ready.Defects identified at early stage.
10Types: Functional, Non-Functional, Regression testing.Types: Path testing, Loop testing, Condition testing.
11Trial and error methods applicable.Data domains and internal boundaries can be better tested.
12Example: Searching on Google using keywords.Example: Input to check and verify loops.

Advantages of Black Box Testing

  • Tester does not need extensive programming knowledge.
  • Efficient for large systems.
  • Tests are from user/client perspective.
  • Finds ambiguities and contradictions in functional specifications.

Advantages of White Box Testing

  • Optimizes code; hidden errors can be identified.
  • Test cases can be easily automated.
  • Early detection of errors improves code quality.
  • Covers most paths and code of the software.

questions.question: Various software testing methods for embedded systems.
questions.answer_html:
Various Software Testing Methods for Embedded Systems

1. Unit Testing

Testing of individual software modules or functions in isolation. Each module is tested independently with known inputs and expected outputs.
  • Verifies each function or driver independently.
  • Uses stubs (dummy called modules) and drivers (dummy calling modules).
  • Commonly done by developers (white box approach).
  • Example: Testing the coin_sorter() function separately.

2. Integration Testing

Testing combined modules together to verify that they interface and interact correctly.
  • Top-down integration: Higher-level modules tested first with stubs for lower-level.
  • Bottom-up integration: Lower-level modules tested first.
  • Finds interface bugs, data format mismatches, and communication errors.

3. System Testing

  • Tests the complete assembled embedded system against its specification requirements.
  • Checks functional and non-functional requirements (performance, power, reliability).
  • Done in real or near-real hardware environment.

4. User Acceptance Testing (UAT)

  • Performed by end-users or clients.
  • Verifies the product meets real-world operational requirements.
  • Final gate before product deployment.

5. Black Box Testing

  • Test software behavior based only on inputs/outputs without knowledge of internal code.
  • Techniques: Equivalence Partitioning, Boundary Value Analysis, Decision Table, State Transition Testing.

6. White Box Testing

  • Test internal code structure, paths, loops, and conditions.
  • Techniques: Path Coverage, Loop Testing, Branch Coverage, Statement Coverage.

7. Regression Testing

  • Re-testing after a bug fix or feature addition to ensure previously working functionality still works.
  • Prevents introduction of new bugs while fixing old ones.

8. Stress / Load Testing

  • Tests system behavior under maximum load or beyond normal operating conditions.
  • Checks for stability, memory leaks, timing failures under stress.

9. Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) Testing

  • Real controller connected to a simulated environment (plant model).
  • Used in automotive and industrial embedded systems.

10. Static Analysis

  • Analysis of code without executing it.
  • MISRA-C checks, lint tools, formal verification.
  • Finds potential bugs at compile/analysis time.

Embedded-Specific Testing Considerations

  • Real-time behavior must be verified (deadline meeting).
  • Interrupt-driven code must be tested under concurrent events.
  • Power-on reset and watchdog timer recovery testing.
  • EEPROM/Flash write endurance testing.
  • Environmental testing (temperature, vibration, humidity).

questions.question: Smart Card Reader system.
questions.answer_html:
Smart Card Reader – Embedded System Design

A Smart Card Reader is an embedded system that interfaces with a smart card (IC card) to read/write data securely, typically used in banking, access control, and identity verification systems.

Components Required

  • Power Supply: Transformer → Rectifier → Regulator (5V / 3.3V).
  • Microcontroller: 8/16-bit MCU (e.g., 8051, ARM Cortex-M). Acts as the system brain.
  • Clock / Oscillator Circuit: Crystal of 11.0592 MHz so that serial communication (UART/RS232) is accurately implemented.
  • Watchdog Timer: Resets the microcontroller if it hangs, preventing abrupt behavior.
  • RS232 / UART Communication Port: For communication with a host system (PC/server). Implemented using the serial port of the microcontroller.
  • Smart Card Reader IC + Antenna: The reader IC interfaces with the smart card's embedded chip (contact or contactless via antenna).
  • Keyboard / Keypad: For PIN entry by the user. When a switch is pressed, the port pin reads '0'; when released, reads '1'.
  • 16×2 LCD Display: Displays messages to the user. Signals: Vcc, GND, Vee (backlight intensity), D0–D7 (data), RS (command/data), RW (read/write), E (enable/latch).
  • Program Memory (Flash/ROM): Stores the firmware.
  • Data Memory (RAM/EEPROM): Stores runtime and persistent data.

Hardware Block Diagram

Software Architecture

  • Smartcard Reader Module: Reads data from the smartcard reader IC, handles authentication protocol.
  • Communication Module: Handles RS232/UART data exchange with host system (PC/server).
  • I/O Module: Manages keyboard input (button press detection) and LCD output (display messages).
  • Watchdog Refresh Module: Periodically resets the watchdog timer to prevent spurious resets.

The system control unit handles I/O (buttons), graphical user interface (LCD control), and can be easily implemented using an 8/16-bit microprocessor/microcontroller.

Working Principle

  1. User inserts smart card → Reader IC detects card via contact/RF antenna.
  2. MCU sends authentication command to card.
  3. User enters PIN via keypad.
  4. MCU verifies PIN against stored value in card.
  5. Result displayed on 16×2 LCD (Authorized / Access Denied).
  6. MCU sends result to host system via RS232.
  7. Watchdog timer monitors for system hang and resets if needed.

questions.question: Design an embedded system (automatic toll collection / vending machine / smart agriculture monitoring) covering specification, component choice, hardware block diagram and software architecture.
questions.answer_html:
Embedded System Design: Automatic Chocolate / Newspaper Vending Machine

Specification Requirements

Functional Requirements:
  • Accept coin insertion from customer.
  • Authenticate coins (detect fake coins using weight and image comparison).
  • Sum up inserted coin values.
  • Dispense product when sufficient amount is inserted.
  • Return change if amount inserted exceeds cost.
  • Refund entire amount if no change is available.
  • Ensure only one item is dispensed per transaction.
  • Display transaction messages on LCD.
Non-Functional Requirements:
  • Performance: Coin authentication < 2 seconds, dispense time < 5 seconds.
  • Power: Mains powered (no battery constraint).
  • Memory: Flash for program, RAM for runtime state.
  • Display: 16×2 or 64×2 LCD for user messages.
  • Reliability: Must handle power failures gracefully; no double dispensing.
  • Safety: No mechanical hazard from roller mechanism.

Component / Hardware Selection

  • Microcontroller: Any 8-bit MCU with sufficient I/O, serial port, and optionally DSP/IP capability for image processing coin recognition. Speed and size not critical (mains power, no space constraint).
  • Coin Sorter: Weighing mechanism + image capture module. Weighs coin and captures both sides to authenticate and determine denomination.
  • Coin Acceptor Vent: IR sensor detects coin insertion.
  • Dispensing Mechanism:
    • Newspaper/Chocolate: Roller mechanism (stepper or servo motor driven) — provides controlled pressure.
    • Opening size matches one item so only one can fall at a time.
  • Refund Mechanism: Coin return actuator.
  • LCD Display: 16×2 or 64×2 LCD — low power, displays multiple messages.
  • IR Sensor: For detecting coin insertion.
  • Motor Driver: Stepper or servo motor driver IC for roller motor.

Hardware Block Diagram

Software Architecture (Modules and Drivers)

  1. Coin Sorter Module:
    • Diagnoses inserted coin for authenticity (image comparison) and value (weight comparison).
    • Forwards value to Coin Summing Module.
  2. Coin Summing Module:
    • Called by Coin Sorter Module.
    • Initializes sum = 0 for each new customer.
    • Keeps adding coin values passed by sorter module.
    • Calls Dispensing Module when sum ≥ cost.
  3. Newspaper/Product and Change Dispensing Module:
    • Dispenses product when exact amount is received.
    • If amount > cost: checks for change availability; dispenses product + returns change.
    • If no change: refunds entire amount, displays inability message.
Drivers Required:
  • Coin Vent Driver: IR sensor driver for coin detection.
  • Motor Driver: Stepper or servo motor driver for roller/dispenser.
  • LCD Driver: Standard 16×2 / 64×2 LCD driver for message display.

FSM of Vending Machine

States: IDLE, COIN_INSERTED, SUM_COMPARE, DISPENSE, REFUND

IDLE:
  → Wait for coin insertion (IR sensor)
  → On coin detected: → COIN_INSERTED

COIN_INSERTED:
  → Authenticate coin (weight + image)
  → Add value to sum
  → Go to SUM_COMPARE

SUM_COMPARE:
  → If sum == cost:   → DISPENSE
  → If sum > cost:   → REFUND (with product)
  → If sum < cost:   → IDLE (wait for more coins)

DISPENSE:
  → Roll out product via motor
  → Reset sum = 0
  → Return to IDLE

REFUND:
  → Calculate change = sum - cost
  → If change available: return change, dispense product
  → If no change: return entire amount, do NOT dispense
  → Display LCD message
  → Return to IDLE

questions.question: Environment monitoring system.
questions.answer_html:
Environment Monitoring System

An Environment Monitoring System is an embedded system that continuously measures environmental parameters (temperature, humidity, CO₂, light, air quality, etc.) and generates alerts or controls actuators when parameters go out of safe range.

Specification Requirements

Functional Requirements:
  • Continuously sense temperature, humidity, CO₂ level, light intensity, air quality (particulate matter).
  • Display current readings on LCD or OLED display.
  • Trigger alerts (buzzer/LED) when thresholds are exceeded.
  • Control actuators: fans, ventilation systems, irrigation (in agriculture).
  • Log data to memory (SD card / EEPROM) for trend analysis.
  • Transmit data wirelessly (Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/LoRa) to cloud or monitoring server.
Non-Functional Requirements:
  • Performance: Sensor reading interval ≤ 1 minute; alert response < 5 seconds.
  • Power: Battery + solar powered (low-power operation mandatory for remote deployment).
  • Memory: EEPROM/SD card for data logging.
  • Reliability: Should work 24×7; weather-resistant enclosure (IP65+).
  • Communication: Wi-Fi/MQTT for cloud upload; Bluetooth for local access.

Component / Hardware Selection

  • Microcontroller: ESP32 (built-in Wi-Fi + Bluetooth, low power modes) or ARM Cortex-M.
  • Sensors:
    • Temperature + Humidity: DHT11 / DHT22 / SHT31
    • CO₂ / Air quality: MQ-135, SCD30 (CO₂ sensor)
    • Light intensity: LDR / BH1750 (digital lux sensor)
    • Rain sensor: Capacitive rain detector
    • Soil moisture: Resistive / capacitive soil sensor (for agriculture)
    • Particulate matter (PM2.5): PMS5003 laser particle counter
  • Signal Conditioning: Op-amp based amplification and filtering for analog sensors; ADC for conversion.
  • Display: 16×2 LCD or OLED (I²C).
  • Communication: ESP32 Wi-Fi module, HC-05 Bluetooth, LoRa module (SX1278) for long range.
  • Actuators: DC fan, relay (for controlling irrigation pump/ventilation), buzzer, LED alerts.
  • Power Supply: Li-ion battery + solar panel + power management IC.
  • Data Storage: microSD card module.

Hardware Block Diagram

Software Architecture

  • Sensor Reading Task: Periodically reads all sensors; converts raw ADC to physical units.
  • Data Processing Task: Compares readings against set thresholds; generates alert flags.
  • Alert/Actuator Control Task: On alert flag: triggers buzzer, activates fan, sends SMS/notification.
  • Display Task: Updates LCD/OLED with current sensor values.
  • Data Logging Task: Writes timestamped readings to microSD or EEPROM.
  • Communication Task: Publishes sensor data to cloud via MQTT over Wi-Fi; or transmits via LoRa.
RTOS Task Structure (if FreeRTOS used):
Task 1: vSensorReadTask   – Priority: HIGH,   Period: 500ms
Task 2: vDataLogTask      – Priority: MEDIUM, Period: 60s
Task 3: vDisplayTask      – Priority: LOW,    Period: 1s
Task 4: vCommTask         – Priority: MEDIUM, Period: 5s
Task 5: vActuatorTask     – Priority: HIGH,   Event-driven (ISR)
